Setup · Table previews · Assessment readiness · Troubleshooting

Start here: one database, one fresh attempt

  1. Use a school-approved SQLite tool. Download base for modelling/guided practice and changed for the independent task. An empty scratch database is used for construction exercises.
  2. Open the .sqlite file directly, or run the matching setup.sql once in a new empty database. Do not run setup over an existing file. Keep an untouched download and work on a named copy.
  3. For each new connection run PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; outside any transaction, then PRAGMA foreign_keys; and confirm 1. This setting is not saved in the database file.
  4. Read the dictionary and preview the rows. Predict first. Run one exercise at a time, compare column names/order, row values/count and sort order, then record the first mismatch. Some tools show only the last SELECT result; run each SELECT separately when comparing multiple result tables.
  5. Changes use fresh disposable copies. After feedback, retry with fresh data; preserve the original attempt. No code runs in this web page and no student work is uploaded.

SQLite conventions: text/date literals use single quotes; dates are fixed-width ISO text; Booleans are constrained 0/1; || concatenates; ALTER TABLE modifies supported schema features. These are explicit teaching choices, not universal DBMS syntax.

At Step 15, use the six-table dictionary and separate seed rows after writing your own schema. The completed setup file is a public reference; inspect it after your independent attempt.

Inspect the supplied tables

The changed dataset adds and changes records; open that database to inspect its full contents before the independent attempt. Download dictionaries and setup files are included in the student ZIP. Duration is a small supplementary numeric fixture for aggregate fluency.

STEP 01 · YEAR 11 · CORE PATHWAY

Choose columns, order rows and remove duplicates

Textbook reading · Dictionary · Base database · Changed database

Start with the supplied four-table equipment database; you do not need to build it before learning queries. SELECT chooses output columns and FROM identifies the table. ORDER BY gives an explicit order; add a secondary key when values tie. DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows. Read the keys and table preview before writing SQL. This step assumes basic table, record, field and primary/foreign-key vocabulary from the linked reading.

Database: y11 / base · fresh copy per exercise.

STEP 02 · YEAR 11 · CORE PATHWAY

Filter and combine conditions before joining

Textbook reading · Dictionary · Base database · Changed database

WHERE retains rows whose condition is true. Use single quotes for text. AND requires both conditions; OR accepts either; parentheses make combinations explicit. NOT negates a condition. BETWEEN includes its endpoints; LIKE uses % for any sequence and _ for one character in SQLite. ISO dates here are fixed-width YYYY-MM-DD text, so lexical comparisons match chronological order. This teaching choice is not a universal date-storage rule.

1. Worked example

Find outstanding loans due before 8 April 2026.

Database: y11 / base · fresh copy per exercise.

SELECT LoanID, DueDate FROM Loan WHERE Returned = 0 AND DueDate < '2026-04-08' ORDER BY DueDate, LoanID;
Worked result and explanation
LoanIDDueDate

STEP 03 · YEAR 11 · CORE PATHWAY

Match a known key in an INNER JOIN

Textbook reading · Dictionary · Base database · Changed database

Read the relationship first: each Loan refers to one Borrower; a Borrower may have several Loans. INNER JOIN pairs rows on matching identifiers. Repeated borrower labels are expected when a person has multiple loans. Qualify columns shared by both tables. Join by corresponding keys, not by similarly shaped names or unrelated row numbers.

1. Worked example

List each loan with its borrower label.

Database: y11 / base · fresh copy per exercise.

SELECT Loan.LoanID, Borrower.BorrowerLabel FROM Loan INNER JOIN Borrower ON Loan.BorrowerID = Borrower.BorrowerID ORDER BY Loan.LoanID;

STEP 04 · YEAR 11 · CORE PATHWAY

Use all five aggregate functions at the right grain

Textbook reading · Dictionary · Base database · Changed database

An aggregate summarises a set of input rows. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN operate on the selected values. Use a small numeric fixture to predict each result by hand. First learn whole-result aggregates without GROUP BY; grouping comes in the Year 12 pathway. For an empty input set COUNT gives zero; these other aggregates give NULL. AS labels an output column; it does not rename a stored field. These simple result labels help compare aggregates before calculated aliases are developed in Year 12.

1. Worked example

Summarise the fixed durations of five practice records.

Database: durations / base · fresh copy per exercise.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS Records, SUM(Days) AS TotalDays, AVG(Days) AS MeanDays, MAX(Days) AS Longest, MIN(Days) AS Shortest FROM Duration;

STEP 05 · YEAR 11 · CORE PATHWAY

Design before CREATE: build three related tables

Textbook reading · Dictionary · Base database · Changed database

Before independent schema construction, complete the linked ER modelling and 1NF -> 2NF -> 3NF practice. Here StudentID determines StudentName, ClubID determines ClubName, and a membership is identified by StudentID plus ClubID. Separate those facts into Student, Club and Membership. An ordinary membership refers to exactly one existing student and club. SQLite uses type affinity; declared types alone do not enforce every domain rule. BOOLEAN and DATE need an explicit storage convention. The model shows inline REFERENCES for foreign keys and a table-level PRIMARY KEY for a pair: neither component alone identifies the relationship record.

1. Worked example

Model a three-table design for devices, skills and dated device-skill records. Inspect the junction key and foreign keys before the independent transfer.

Database: scratch / base · fresh copy per exercise.

CREATE TABLE Device (DeviceID TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL, Label TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE Skill (SkillID TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL, SkillName TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE DeviceSkill (DeviceID TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES Device(DeviceID), SkillID TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES Skill(SkillID), RecordedOn TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY(DeviceID, SkillID));

Verification queries

SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' ORDER BY name;
SELECT name, type, pk FROM pragma_table_info('DeviceSkill') ORDER BY cid;
PRAGMA foreign_key_list(DeviceSkill);

3. Changed independent task

From the stated dependencies, create Student(StudentID, StudentName), Club(ClubID, ClubName), Membership(StudentID, ClubID, JoinedOn). Use required TEXT fields, a composite Membership primary key and both foreign keys. JoinedOn stores ISO date text. Explain why names belong in the parent tables.

Database: scratch / changed · fresh copy per exercise.

Record prediction → run / hand trace → actual result → first mismatch → correction → fresh retry.

Reveal reference SQL and expected result after your attempt
CREATE TABLE Student (StudentID TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL, StudentName TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE Club (ClubID TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL, ClubName TEXT NOT NULL);

STEP 15 · YEAR 12 · CORE PATHWAY

Independent six-table construction and constraint checks

Textbook reading · Dictionary · Base database · Changed database

Use the supplied dictionary and relationship list to implement Instructor, Workshop, Session, Member, Booking and Attendance in an empty database. The independent construction has six tables, exceeding the five-table minimum for Year 12. Define the whole composite Booking key and matching Attendance foreign key. Capacity must be an integer greater than zero; attendance is an integer 0 or 1. Use the source dictionary rather than copying a finished schema before the first attempt. typeof checks SQLite's stored value type; the positive-value comparison separately rules out zero and negative capacity. length counts characters; trim removes surrounding spaces. The worked Label constraint demonstrates how to enforce a trimmed non-empty length limit.

1. Worked example

Demonstrate positive integer capacity and a trimmed label length of 1..60 on one practice table.

Database: scratch / base · fresh copy per exercise.

CREATE TABLE Sample (ID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Capacity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(typeof(Capacity)='integer' AND Capacity > 0), Label TEXT NOT NULL CHECK(length(trim(Label)) BETWEEN 1 AND 60));

STEP 17 · YEAR 12 · SUPPORT BOOKLET + ENRICHMENT

Support-booklet HAVING and optional LEFT JOIN

Textbook reading · Dictionary · Base database · Changed database

HAVING appears in the official additional syllabus support booklet (printed p22); learn group filtering after core GROUP BY/aggregate work. LEFT JOIN is additional to the explicitly listed INNER JOIN syntax. It preserves unmatched left-side rows with NULL right-side fields. COUNT(right_key) ignores those NULLs while COUNT(*) counts the preserved row; IS NULL tests missing values. This step combines a support-booklet skill and an extension: teach each part before including it in the locally issued scope. See the scope guide for the distinction.

1. Worked example

Include sessions with no bookings and count real booking keys.

Database: y12 / base · fresh copy per exercise.

SELECT s.SessionID, COUNT(b.MemberID) AS Bookings FROM Session AS s LEFT JOIN Booking AS b ON b.SessionID = s.SessionID GROUP BY s.SessionID ORDER BY s.SessionID;

STEP 18 · YEAR 12 · IMPLEMENTATION SUPPORT · ACID CORE

SQLite transaction implementation for ACID

Textbook reading · Dictionary · Base database · Changed database

Supporting application/reliability practice. A transaction can keep related changes together. BEGIN starts the boundary, COMMIT accepts it, and ROLLBACK cancels uncommitted changes. Use explicit boundaries in a disposable SQLite tool; other drivers may manage transactions differently. Enable foreign keys before BEGIN. A second BEGIN inside an open transaction fails. After an error, choose an explicit rollback/recovery action rather than assuming every earlier statement was undone.

1. Worked example

Change capacity inside a transaction, then cancel it.

Database: y12 / base · fresh copy per exercise.

BEGIN;
UPDATE Session SET Capacity = 8 WHERE SessionID = 'S01';
ROLLBACK;

Verification queries

Teacher checkpoint: practise before assessment

These are formative readiness checks, not a replacement assessment outline or automatic proof of readiness. Before assessing an operation, record its teaching, a changed independent attempt, feedback and a fresh retry. If that evidence is absent, teach/practise it first or remove it from the issued task scope. The public references are not secure assessment questions.

Year 11: complete Steps 01–08, including independent three-table creation and every aggregate. Year 12: retrieve Year 11 skills, then complete Steps 09–16, including independent six-table construction, change/constraint tests and import decisions. Step 17 combines support-booklet HAVING with optional LEFT JOIN. Step 18 illustrates explicit SQLite transaction commands; ACID remains required knowledge. Teach relevant support/implementation material before local assessment. If your local practical is in Week 10, schedule its required preparation before that date; later project teaching does not count retrospectively. Keep the general textbook calendar adaptable.

Troubleshooting: isolate the first mismatch

No such table / column
Check the open filename, database variant and dictionary spelling. A new empty scratch file has no teaching tables until you create them.
Table already exists / duplicate key during setup
Setup is a once-only load, not a reset script. Open a new empty file or restore the untouched download.
Foreign key insert unexpectedly succeeds
Query PRAGMA foreign_keys on that connection. Enable it before BEGIN, then retry on a fresh copy.
FOREIGN KEY / NOT NULL / UNIQUE / CHECK error
Identify the exact parent, missing value, duplicate key or domain rule. Expected invalid-test errors are learning evidence. Compare stored rows after the error; do not remove the constraint to make the test pass.
Too many rows or inflated totals
Inspect the join key and row grain. Add one table at a time. DISTINCT is not a general repair for a wrong join.
Empty result
Check the supplied rows and each WHERE condition separately. No rows can be the correct answer.
Rows in a different order
Add the required ORDER BY and tie-breaker. Storage/display order is not an ordering contract.
Unexpected NULL / count of one for no bookings
Use IS NULL. COUNT(column) ignores NULL while COUNT(*) counts preserved outer-join rows. Do not silently treat unknown attendance as absence.
Fraction is zero / concatenation fails
Check real versus integer division, the SQLite || operator, quoting and NULL operands.
Cannot start a transaction within a transaction / database locked
Check your tool's transaction state and other open editing connections. Commit only intended work or roll back the practice transaction; close the extra writer. Reopen a fresh copy if the state is uncertain.
Missing or changed rows on a later task
Do not reuse a mutated file. Restore base/changed as specified. Reference expectations always start fresh.

Primary technical references: SQLite SELECT, foreign keys, ALTER TABLE, transactions.
